Do not use the variable height list for a fixed-height test. Use FixedSizeList when every row has the same itemSize.

steps.do: Build the production bundle with the project build script.
Serve the built output on port 4173 with the preview script in the background.
Run Lighthouse on the performance category only and write the result to lh-layout.json.
Read the performance score from the JSON file with jq.

K-016285.example: After npm run build, Lighthouse scores http://localhost:4173 and jq prints 0.94 for the performance category. A score of 0.9 or higher passes the gate.
K-016285.check: jq prints a number of 0.9 or higher, and lh-layout.json exists and is valid JSON.
traps: Small models often run Lighthouse against the dev server on port 5173. Dev builds are not representative, so always measure the production preview.
Lighthouse scores vary between runs. Run it three times and compare the median, not one result.

steps.do: Confirm the react-hooks lint rule is enabled in the ESLint config file.
Run ESLint on the layout folder and fail on any warning.
If ESLint reports a missing dependency, add that variable to the array in the useLayoutEffect call that reads layout measurements.
Run ESLint again to confirm the warning is gone.

K-016286.example: src/layout/Measure.tsx had useLayoutEffect(() => {...}, []) while it read width from a width prop, and ESLint reported react-hooks/exhaustive-deps. Adding width to the array makes the second ESLint run exit with code 0 and no output.
K-016286.check: npx eslint exits with code 0 and prints no warnings or errors, and rg prints a line that contains exhaustive-deps.
traps: Small models often silence the exhaustive-deps warning with an eslint-disable comment. Fix the dependency array instead, because a stale measurement causes layout bugs.
Do not put an object or array literal in the dependency list. A new reference on every render makes the effect run on every commit.

steps.do: Install size-limit and its app preset as dev dependencies.
Add a size-limit entry to package.json that points at the built layout chunk in dist/assets and sets the limit to 60 kB.
Build the production bundle so the chunk exists.
Run size-limit and fail if any entry is over its limit.

K-016287.example: The package.json entry points at dist/assets/Shell-*.js with a limit of 60 kB, and npx size-limit reports Size: 41.8 kB gzipped. The run exits with code 0 because 41.8 kB is under the 60 kB limit.
K-016287.check: npx size-limit prints 'Size limit: 60 kB' and a measured size below 60 kB, and it exits with code 0.
traps: Small models often measure the whole dist folder, which includes vendor code and gives a number that is too large. Point the entry at the layout chunk only.
Do not raise the limit when the check fails. Remove the unused import or split the component with React.lazy.

steps.do: Confirm ratatui is a dependency in Cargo.toml.
Find the files that define the navigation widget.
Record the number of nav items in the plan as a number.
Measure the release build time as the baseline.
Write the budget in the plan: one key press must produce one frame within 16ms.

K-016288.example: Cargo.toml line 12 shows ratatui = "0.29", and src/nav.rs holds 9 nav items, so the plan sets a 16ms key-to-frame budget. The release build baseline is recorded as the time cargo prints.
K-016288.check: grep prints a line like `12:ratatui = "0.29"`, and cargo build --release ends with `Finished release` in its output.
traps: Small models often skip the grep and guess the ratatui version.
A budget written as fast cannot be checked later; it needs a number like 16ms.
Running cargo build without --release measures the wrong profile.

steps.do: Read the current terminal width to set the nav column budget.
Read the current terminal height to set the row budget.
Find every wrefresh call in the nav source to count the flushes a key press causes.
Write the plan: the nav uses wnoutrefresh for each panel and one doupdate per key press.
Set the nav panel to 20 columns wide and at most 22 rows tall.

K-016289.example: tput prints 80 and 24, and rg finds 3 wrefresh calls in src/nav.c. The plan replaces them with wnoutrefresh and a single doupdate, so each key press makes 1 terminal flush.
K-016289.check: rg prints the 3 wrefresh lines in src/nav.c, so the plan has a starting count to reduce to 1 per key press.
traps: Small models often assume an 80-column terminal without asking tput.
wrefresh flushes each window separately; plan wnoutrefresh and doupdate instead.
Do not set a row count larger than tput lines reports.

steps.do: Check the terminal size the app runs in.
Compute the total cell count by multiplying the width and height from the previous outputs.
Find where the nav bar is laid out with Rect areas.
Write the plan: a nav key press changes at most 200 cells, all inside the nav area.
Run the existing nav tests to confirm the baseline passes.

K-016290.example: tput reports 120 columns and 40 rows, so the screen has 4800 cells. The plan caps a nav key press at 200 changed cells, the 20x10 nav area.
K-016290.check: cargo test nav ends with `test result: ok`, and the plan lists a changed-cell limit under 200.
traps: Small models often redraw the full frame, which can change all 4800 cells.
ratatui diffs buffers, so the budget counts changed cells, not drawn widgets.
A cell budget without a measured width and height cannot be checked.

steps.do: Find the file that holds the nav entries.
Count the lines in the nav data file to size the menu.
Run the existing nav benchmark to get a baseline median.
Write the plan: loading and drawing 500 nav items takes under 200ms at the median.

K-016291.example: wc reports 512 lines in src/nav_items.txt, and the benchmark median is 240ms, above the 200ms budget. The plan requires a lazy load of visible rows only, to get under 200ms.
K-016291.check: cargo bench prints a median time per run, and the plan records a target of 200ms or less that the benchmark must reach.
traps: Small models often budget for the whole list, when only the visible rows need drawing.
A benchmark without a recorded baseline cannot show improvement.
Counting lines is not the same as counting items if entries span several lines.

steps.do: Find where the event loop reads or polls key events.
Check which crossterm version Cargo.toml pins.
Write the plan: drain all pending key events with event::poll(Duration::ZERO) before one draw.
Set the target: 30 held-key events per second produce at most 30 draws.
Check that the event loop compiles before any code is written.

K-016292.example: rg finds event::poll(Duration::from_millis(50)) at src/main.rs:88, and Cargo.toml pins crossterm = "0.28". The plan drains queued keys first, so a held key at 30 events per second produces at most 30 draws.
K-016292.check: rg prints `src/main.rs:88`, and cargo check ends with `Finished` with no errors.
traps: Small models often use event::read, which blocks and skips the drain loop.
Draw once per drained batch, not once per key event.
A 50ms poll timeout adds latency to every key; Duration::ZERO only drains what is already queued.

steps.do: Compile the Tailwind source file into a minified stylesheet.
Count how many times the peer-invalid variant appears in the output.
Confirm the output file is not empty.

K-016293.example: The signup form has an input with class peer and a p tag with class hidden peer-invalid:block that holds the email error text. The minified CSS is one line, so grep reports 1 when the selector is present.
K-016293.check: Step 1 ends with a Done line and no errors, grep prints 1 or more, and test exits silently with status 0.
traps: If the input lacks the peer class, peer-invalid never matches and the error stays hidden.
Tailwind v4 uses @import "tailwindcss" instead of @tailwind directives, so check the version in package.json first.
If the dist folder does not exist, the build output fails to write; run mkdir -p dist first.

steps.do: Install the Chromium browser that Playwright uses.
Run the signup validation spec on the Chromium project.
List all discovered tests to confirm the spec file was found.

K-016294.example: The spec loads /signup and asserts the element with id email-error is hidden. It types abc into an input of type email, presses Tab, then asserts the element is visible with the text Enter a valid email. The run should report 2 passed.
K-016294.check: The spec output ends with 2 passed, and the --list output includes signup-validation.spec.ts.
traps: An email field is not invalid until a value is typed, so the test must fill a value before checking for the error.
The error appears on blur, not on each keystroke, so checking visibility before blur gives a false failure.
Hidden error text still exists in the DOM, so assert toBeHidden rather than counting the element.

steps.do: Start the Vite dev server on port 5173 in its own tmux window.
Run the touch target spec at a 375px viewport width.
Scan the signup page with axe against WCAG 2.2 AA rules.

K-016295.example: Each input uses min-h-11, which is 2.75rem or 44px at the default 16px root size. The spec reads the boundingBox height of every input and expects at least 44 for each one.
K-016295.check: The Playwright run reports passed, and axe reports 0 target-size violations.
traps: h-8 gives 32px, which is below the 44px minimum even though it looks fine on desktop.
min-h-11 depends on the default spacing scale, so a custom spacing override changes the pixel value.
Vite must be running before the spec starts, or every test fails with a connection error.

steps.do: Create the reports directory for the audit output.
Build the production bundle.
Serve the built site on port 4173 in its own tmux window.
Run a Lighthouse accessibility audit on the signup page and save it as JSON.
Read the accessibility score from the JSON report.

K-016296.example: The signup page passes if jq prints 0.96, which is the category score on a 0 to 1 scale. The gate for this card is 0.90 or higher.
K-016296.check: jq prints a number of 0.90 or higher.
traps: Lighthouse JSON scores run from 0 to 1, not 0 to 100 like the report UI, so compare against 0.90 and not 90.
vite preview blocks the shell, so start it in tmux before running the audit.
Dev server audits give unstable scores, so audit the built output on port 4173.

steps.do: Confirm the overflow spec reads the document scroll width.
Run the no-overflow spec at 320px and 375px viewports.
Confirm the form grid starts with a single column at the base breakpoint.

K-016297.example: The form uses grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2, so it stacks on a 320px screen. The spec sets the viewport width to 320 and asserts document.documentElement.scrollWidth is 320 or less.
K-016297.check: grep prints the line number containing scrollWidth, the Playwright run reports 2 passed for the two viewports, and grep finds grid-cols-1 in SignupForm.tsx.
traps: Using grid-cols-2 without a base breakpoint forces two columns at 320px and causes sideways scrolling.
Long error messages in a narrow column need break-words, or they widen the page.
Checking scrollWidth only at the default desktop viewport proves nothing about small phones.

steps.do: Run the error-state spec that submits the empty form to show all errors.
Run the axe color-contrast rule against the page in its error state.
Confirm the error text color class is used in the form source.

K-016298.example: Error text uses text-red-700, which is #b91c1c. Against white (#ffffff) that is about 6.47:1, above the 4.5:1 minimum for normal text.
K-016298.check: The spec reports passed, axe reports 0 color-contrast violations, and grep prints a line number containing text-red-700.
traps: text-red-500 is #ef4444, about 3.76:1 on white, which fails the 4.5:1 minimum for small text.
Color alone is not enough for an error; the message text must say what went wrong.
The URL contains a ? that bash can glob, so wrap the URL in single quotes.

steps.do: Find where the app root is rendered in src/main.tsx so you know where to wrap it with Profiler from react.
Wrap the layout root in the Profiler component from react in src/main.tsx, giving it id AppShell and an onRender callback.
Create the empty test file src/layout/Grid.perf.test.tsx, then write a test that dispatches 10 resize events and counts the onRender calls.
Run the perf test through the project test script.
Add an assertion that fails the test if the commit count is above 2, which means the resize handler is not batched. Then confirm the assertion is in the file.

K-016299.example: Grid.perf.test.tsx fires 10 resize events on a 200-card grid, and the Profiler callback records commits=2 after requestAnimationFrame batching is added to the resize handler. Before batching, the same test records commits=10.
K-016299.check: npm test prints '1 passed', and the test log shows commits=2 or fewer for 10 resize events.
traps: Small models often count renders when they should count commits. A render can happen without a commit, so count only onRender calls.
Profiler timings are only reported in development builds or the profiling build. Do not read timing numbers from a minified production bundle.

steps.do: Confirm the placeholder option has an empty value attribute.
Count select elements that carry the required attribute.
Run the Playwright test that submits with the placeholder still selected.
In that test, assert the select has valueMissing set to true and that no submit event fires.

K-016300.example: form.html has a select id plan with required and an option value of empty string labelled Choose a plan, so grep prints line 14. The Playwright test expects 1 passed and asserts valueMissing is true on the first submit attempt.
K-016300.check: grep prints one line for the empty value option, and npx playwright test prints 1 passed with 0 failed.
traps: A placeholder with no value attribute submits its text, so valueMissing stays false.
Checking only the :valid pseudo-class in CSS does not prove the form was blocked from submitting.
Use an empty string as the value, not the option text, or the required check passes wrongly.

steps.do: Count the setCustomValidity calls in the script to confirm one sets the message and one clears it.
Run the Playwright test that selects a valid option and reads validationMessage.
In that test, assert validationMessage equals the empty string after the change event.

K-016301.example: app.js calls setCustomValidity with Pick a plan when the value is empty, and calls it with an empty string inside the change listener, so grep prints 2. The spec selects the Basic option and expects validationMessage to be an empty string.
K-016301.check: grep prints 2, and npx playwright test prints 1 passed with 0 failed.
traps: Forgetting to clear the custom message leaves the select permanently invalid after a correct choice.
Listening only to the input event on select can miss updates in some browsers, so listen to change.
Calling setCustomValidity once at page load and never again leaves stale messages on screen.

steps.do: Find the error text color declaration in the stylesheet.
Run the Playwright test that forces the invalid state and runs axe color-contrast on the error element.
In that test, assert the color-contrast rule reports 0 violations for the error message.

K-016302.example: errors.css sets .field-error color to #b00020 on a white background, which gives a ratio of about 6.5:1. The spec triggers the invalid state and expects 0 color-contrast violations.
K-016302.check: grep shows the .field-error color line, and npx playwright test prints 1 passed with 0 failed.
traps: Using a light red such as #ff8080 on white falls well below 4.5:1 even though it looks readable.
Checking contrast only on the valid state misses the error color entirely.
Large text allows 3:1, but error text at 16px or 1rem needs the full 4.5:1.

steps.do: Confirm the stylesheet sets a minimum height of 44px on the select.
Run the Playwright test at a 390 by 844 viewport and read the select bounding box.
In that test, assert the boundingBox height is at least 44 pixels.

K-016303.example: forms.css sets select min-height to 44px, and the spec at 390 by 844 reads a boundingBox height of 46. The spec expects the height to be at least 44 and passes.
K-016303.check: grep prints the min-height 44px line, and npx playwright test prints 1 passed with a reported height of 44 or more.
traps: A 1rem font size alone does not set the tap target, so padding or min-height must be set explicitly.
Measuring at desktop width hides the touch sizing problem that shows on phones.
Using 40px fails the 44px target even when it looks close enough.

steps.do: Count occurrences of novalidate in the form markup, which should be zero so native validation runs.
Run the Playwright test that clicks submit with the select empty and checks that the request never fires.
Run Lighthouse on the form page limited to the accessibility category and write JSON output.
Read the accessibility score from the Lighthouse JSON file.

K-016304.example: form.html has no novalidate attribute, so grep prints 0. The Lighthouse JSON reports an accessibility score of 1, which jq prints as 1.
K-016304.check: grep prints 0, npx playwright test prints 1 passed, and jq prints 1.
traps: Adding novalidate to the form disables native checks and lets an empty select submit.
A score below 1 means at least one audit failed, so the output must be read, not assumed.
The Playwright check must wait for the network request to be absent, not just for the click to finish.

steps.do: Build the production bundle for the onboarding route.
In a second terminal, serve the built app on port 4173.
Run the 375 pixel mobile viewport spec.
Confirm the spec compares scrollWidth with the viewport width.

K-016305.example: At 375px the spec reads document.documentElement.scrollWidth and expects it to equal 375. A page 390px wide fails with a 15px overflow.
K-016305.check: The Playwright run prints '1 passed' and exits with code 0, and grep prints a count of 1 or more.
traps: Testing at the default 1280px desktop size proves nothing about phones. The viewport must come from the mobile-375 project in playwright.config.ts. Checking CSS rules alone does not show overflow, so…

steps.do: Count the wizard button class names in the component.
Run the touch target spec that reads each button's bounding box.
Run axe against the onboarding route with WCAG 2.2 AA rules.
Confirm the spec asserts a minimum height of 44.

K-016306.example: The Next button measures 48px tall and Back measures 44px, so each boundingBox height is at least 44. The spec fails if Skip measures 40px.
K-016306.check: Grep reports 3 or more wizard-btn matches, Playwright prints '3 passed', and axe reports no target-size violations.
traps: Measuring a wrapper div instead of the button itself gives a false pass. Padding counts toward boundingBox height, so a short label can still pass. Do not use 40px as the minimum.

steps.do: List the media queries in the wizard component with line numbers.
Run the Vitest unit spec for the wizard component.
Type-check the Vue single-file components.

K-016307.example: Grep shows @media (min-width: 768px) at line 84, and the Vitest spec mocks useMediaQuery to return true at 768. The expected layout class is wizard--row.
K-016307.check: Grep prints one line containing 768px, Vitest prints 'Tests 4 passed (4)', and vue-tsc exits with no output.
traps: jsdom has no real layout, so Vitest cannot measure CSS widths; use Playwright for that. Forgetting that useMediaQuery returns a ref means tests compare the ref object, not true or false.

steps.do: Create the reports directory for Lighthouse output.
Run Lighthouse in mobile form factor against the preview build.
Read the accessibility score from the JSON report.

K-016308.example: The jq output is 0.96, which is above the 0.90 threshold. A score of 0.82 means the wizard needs fixes before it ships.
K-016308.check: jq prints a number between 0 and 1 that is 0.90 or higher, and the file reports/onboarding-mobile.json exists.
traps: Lighthouse scores run from 0 to 1, not 0 to 100. Running against the dev server gives unreliable numbers, so use the preview build on port 4173.

steps.do: Count the transition declarations in the wizard component.
Confirm the component handles reduced motion.
Run the timing spec that measures the step change duration.

K-016309.example: The timing spec records 120ms from clicking Next to the new step being visible, and expects a value of 200 or less. With prefers-reduced-motion set, the expected duration is 0ms.
K-016309.check: Grep prints 1 or more for each pattern, and Playwright prints '2 passed', one for normal motion and one for reduced motion.
traps: The Vue Transition duration in JavaScript can differ from the CSS duration, so the test should measure the rendered result. Measure after requestAnimationFrame, not immediately after the click.

steps.do: Count the named projects in the Playwright config.
List the tests Playwright finds in the responsive spec.
Run the responsive spec across all projects.

K-016310.example: The config defines 4 projects at 320, 375, 768, and 1280 pixels. The spec has 3 tests, so the run reports 12 tests across 4 projects.
K-016310.check: Grep prints 4 or more, the --list output shows 3 tests per project, and the final run prints '12 passed' with exit code 0.
traps: A spec with 3 tests in 4 projects runs 12 times, not 3, so compare totals against the project count. Skipped tests show as skipped, not passed, so read the summary line.

steps.do: List the routes to see whether a root layout already exists.
Read the current root layout if one exists.
Count the files that render the children snippet.
Plan a svelte:head block in the root layout with a meta tag named color-scheme and content light dark.
Plan one theme toggle button with an aria-label and a minimum size of 44px by 44px.

K-016311.example: The ls output shows one +layout.svelte, so the plan puts the theme toggle and the svelte:head meta there. The toggle is 44px by 44px with aria-label set to Toggle theme.
K-016311.check: rg -c prints one line per file that renders children with a count after the colon, and the plan names exactly one root layout that wraps all routes.
traps: Small models add the theme toggle to every page. Put it once in src/routes/+layout.svelte.
Svelte 5 uses {@render children()} instead of the old slot element. Do not plan a slot element in a runes-mode layout.

steps.do: In a separate terminal, start a static server on port 8080 with python3 -m http.server 8080 and leave it running.
Run axe against the order page and fail on any WCAG 2.1 AA violation.
Confirm the select has aria-describedby pointing to the error element id.

K-016312.example: The curl step prints HTTP/1.0 200 OK. The select id shipping has aria-describedby set to shipping-error, and the element with id shipping-error holds the text Choose a shipping method. The axe run reports 0 violations and exits with code 0.
K-016312.check: curl prints a line containing 200, npx axe prints 0 violations and exit code 0, and grep prints the aria-describedby line for shipping.
traps: An error text element without a matching id gives a screen reader nothing to announce.
Setting aria-invalid to true without showing visible error text fails the intent of the check.
Running axe on a page before the error state is rendered only tests the valid state.

steps.do: List every Svelte component and stylesheet under src.
Count hard-coded hex colors in the source tree.
Find files that already read the system color scheme.
Confirm the Playwright runner is installed so later contrast checks can run.
Write the list of color roles (surface, text, border, accent) into docs/theme-plan.md.

K-016313.example: The count shows 14 hex colors across 6 files, so the plan maps them to 4 roles with one light and one dark value each. Each role becomes one CSS custom property such as --color-surface.
K-016313.check: The rg -c output lists each file with a nonzero count, npx playwright --version exits 0, and the plan lists 4 or fewer roles that cover all 14 colors.
traps: Small models invent token names without counting the existing colors first. Always run the count before naming tokens.
Do not plan a token for every hex value. Group values into roles.

steps.do: Show the document shell that SvelteKit renders.
Confirm the head placeholder exists exactly once.
Check whether a theme attribute is already set in the shell.
Confirm the Playwright runner is installed so first paint can be timed against the 200ms budget.
Plan an inline script in the head that reads localStorage key theme, falls back to matchMedia prefers-color-scheme dark, and sets data-theme on document.documentElement.
Record in the plan that the storage read is wrapped in try and catch for blocked storage.

K-016314.example: The grep count prints 1, so the plan adds one inline script above %sveltekit.head% that sets data-theme to dark or light. The storage read is wrapped in try and catch so private mode does not throw. The script must finish before the 200ms first-paint budget.
K-016314.check: grep -c prints 1 for the placeholder, grep -n for data-theme prints nothing before the build, and npx playwright --version exits 0.
traps: Small models put theme logic in onMount, which runs after first paint and causes a flash. The script belongs in the head of app.html.
Do not skip the try and catch around localStorage, because some browsers throw on access.

steps.do: Confirm the project uses Svelte 5 by reading the svelte version in devDependencies.
Check that no legacy writable theme store already exists.
Create the folder for the theme module.
Create the module file with the .svelte.js extension so runes compile outside components.
Confirm the module file exists after the touch command.
Confirm the Playwright runner is installed so the module can be checked in a browser.
Plan the module to export one $state value named mode with light, dark, or system, and one $derived value named resolved.

K-016315.example: The jq output starts with ^5, so the plan uses $state for mode and $derived for resolved. The file lives at src/lib/theme/theme.svelte.js and is imported through $lib/theme/theme.svelte.js.
K-016315.check: jq prints a version starting with ^5 or higher, test -f exits 0 after the touch command, and npx playwright --version exits 0.
traps: Small models name the file theme.js, so $state will not compile. The file must end in .svelte.js.
Do not import the store with a long relative path when $lib is configured.

steps.do: Create the docs folder for planning notes.
Create the plan file that will hold the contrast table.
Record in the plan that body text needs at least 4.5:1 contrast against its background.
Record that large text (24px regular or 18.66px bold) and UI borders need at least 3:1 contrast.
Confirm the Playwright runner is installed so the contrast pairs can be checked in a browser.
Count the table rows that start with a pipe once the table is written.

K-016316.example: The table lists 6 text pairs at 4.5:1 and 2 border pairs at 3:1, giving 8 planned pairs. The plan file therefore needs at least 8 pipe-starting rows, so rg -c must print a count of 8 or more.
K-016316.check: rg -c prints a count at least equal to the number of planned color pairs, and npx playwright --version exits 0.
traps: Small models apply 4.5:1 to everything. Large text and non-text UI only need 3:1.
Do not pick palette values before the budget is written, or the plan drifts from the requirement.

steps.do: Find every CSS custom property declared in the app stylesheet.
Count the custom property declarations.
Check whether a data-theme selector already exists.
Check for hard-coded white or black colors in components that will need overrides.
Confirm the Playwright runner is installed so the dark block can be checked in a browser.
Plan a dark block that redefines every light token under the selector html[data-theme='dark'].

K-016317.example: The count prints 12 for the stylesheet, so the plan writes 12 dark values in one html[data-theme='dark'] block. Hard-coded #fff in 3 components is converted to var(--color-surface).
K-016317.check: The dark block defines the same number of tokens as the light declaration count printed by rg -c, and npx playwright --version exits 0.
traps: Small models redefine only the colors they noticed and miss tokens, so some text stays light on a light background. Count tokens first and match the count.
Do not rely only on @media prefers-color-scheme when the user can toggle, because the data-theme selector must win.

steps.do: Create the component folder.
Write src/components/AppButton.vue with script setup, defineProps for label as String and disabled as Boolean, and one root button element.
Do not add watch, onMounted, or ref inside AppButton.vue, so the component stays a pure render.
Run the Vue type checker on the project.
Build the app to confirm the component compiles.

K-016318.example: AppButton.vue declares label as String and disabled as Boolean with defineProps and renders one button element. A parent writes <AppButton label='Save' /> and npm run build prints no errors.
K-016318.check: npm run build exits with code 0 and prints 'built in' with no warnings that mention AppButton.vue.
traps: Adding watch or onMounted to a button adds work on every mount. Declaring props as an object literal inside the template creates new objects on each render.

steps.do: Open AppButton.vue and define a computed named buttonClass that returns a string built from the variant and size props.
Bind it with :class='buttonClass' on the root button element and remove any inline style objects.
Add a spec that mounts the button with variant 'primary' and checks that the class list contains btn-primary.
Run the spec file.
Lint the component file.

K-016319.example: The computed buttonClass returns 'btn btn-primary btn-md' when variant is 'primary' and size is 'md'. The spec mounts with variant 'primary' and expects the class list to contain btn-primary.
K-016319.check: The vitest run reports 1 passed and 0 failed, and eslint prints no errors.
traps: A computed that returns a new object still recalculates when any dependency changes, so keep its inputs to primitive props. Small models often put class logic in a method called from the template, wh…

steps.do: In ButtonGrid.vue, put v-for, :key set to item.id, and v-memo set to the fields that affect the button output, such as item.label and item.selected, on each AppButton.
Add a benchmark spec that mounts 500 buttons and counts child render calls with a spy.
Run the benchmark spec to measure the render count.
Run the Vue type checker.
Build the app.

K-016320.example: v-for='item in items' :key='item.id' v-memo='[item.label, item.selected]' stops 500 buttons from re-rendering when only one item's selected flag changes. After toggling one item the spy count rises by 1, not by 500.
